title: Geoscience
summary: Reading the Earth's record and its moving parts. Deep time and plate tectonics are the thresholds: once a learner can think in millions of years and in slowly flowing solid rock, mountains, earthquakes, ores and climate history all fit one story.
sources: Stein & Wysession: An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure
Ruddiman: Earth's Climate: Past and Future

nodes.label: Minerals, Rocks & the Rock Cycle
nodes.summary: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks and the processes that turn one into another.
nodes.outcome: Explain each path through the rock cycle.
nodes.check: How does a sedimentary rock become a metamorphic one?
nodes.answer: Burial under heat and pressure recrystallises it without melting.

nodes.label: Stratigraphy & Relative Dating
nodes.summary: Superposition, cross-cutting relations and fossils order events without numbers.
nodes.outcome: Order the events in a geological cross-section.
nodes.check: In undisturbed sedimentary layers, which layer is oldest?

nodes.label: Deep Time & Radiometric Dating
nodes.summary: Radioactive decay is a clock: half-lives give absolute ages and reveal an Earth 4.5 billion years old. Troublesome because human intuition stops at thousands of years.
nodes.outcome: Compute an age from the fraction of parent isotope remaining.
nodes.check: A rock retains 25% of its original parent isotope. How many half-lives have passed?

nodes.label: "Carbon-14 dates dinosaur bones"
nodes.summary: C-14's half-life is about 5,730 years, so it is useless beyond roughly 50,000 years; old rocks are dated with long-lived isotopes such as U–Pb.
nodes.outcome: Choose a dating method suited to an age range.
nodes.check: Why can't carbon-14 date a 66-million-year-old dinosaur bone?
nodes.answer: C-14's half-life is about 5,730 years; after roughly 50,000 years too little remains to measure.

nodes.label: Earth's Interior
nodes.summary: Crust, mantle, outer and inner core, mapped by seismic waves.
nodes.outcome: Use seismic shadow zones to infer the core's structure.
nodes.check: How do we know Earth's outer core is liquid?
nodes.answer: S-waves cannot travel through liquid, so they vanish in a shadow zone behind the core.

nodes.label: Plate Tectonics
nodes.summary: Rigid plates move over a slowly flowing mantle; their boundaries make mountains, ocean basins, earthquakes and volcanoes.
nodes.outcome: Explain features at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.
nodes.answer: Mantle convection, with slab pull from sinking plates (and ridge push) doing most of the work.

nodes.label: "Plates float on a sea of molten magma"
nodes.summary: The mantle is solid rock that flows extremely slowly; melt forms only locally.
nodes.check: Is the mantle beneath the plates mostly liquid magma?
nodes.answer: No: it is solid rock that flows very slowly over geological time; melt is only local.

nodes.label: Earthquakes & Seismic Waves
nodes.summary: Faults slip, P and S waves travel at different speeds, and the S–P gap gives distance.
nodes.outcome: Locate an epicentre from three seismograms.
nodes.check: A station records P and S arrivals 20 s apart. With vp = 6 km/s and vs = 3.5 km/s, how far away is the earthquake?

nodes.label: "Magnitude 6 is twice magnitude 3"
nodes.summary: Magnitude is logarithmic: each step is about 32 times more energy.
nodes.check: How much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?

nodes.label: Volcanoes & Magma
nodes.summary: Magma composition sets viscosity and gas content, and so eruption style.
nodes.outcome: Predict eruption style from magma composition.
nodes.check: Why do silica-rich magmas erupt explosively?
nodes.answer: High silica makes them viscous, so gas can't escape until pressure builds and shatters the magma.

nodes.label: Erosion & Landscapes
nodes.summary: Rivers, glaciers, wind and mass wasting shape the surface.
nodes.check: Why are V-shaped valleys usually cut by rivers and U-shaped valleys by glaciers?
nodes.answer: Rivers cut down narrowly at the bed; glaciers erode the whole floor and sides of the valley.

nodes.label: Earth Resources
nodes.summary: Ores, groundwater, hydrocarbons and the geology that concentrates them.
nodes.outcome: Explain how a petroleum trap forms.
nodes.check: Why do oil and gas accumulate in traps?
nodes.answer: They are buoyant and migrate upward until an impermeable cap rock stops them.

nodes.label: Geohazards & Risk
nodes.summary: Earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes and tsunamis; risk as hazard × exposure × vulnerability.
nodes.outcome: Assess risk for a town near an active fault.
nodes.check: Why is risk not the same as hazard?
nodes.answer: Risk combines the hazard with exposure and vulnerability: a big quake in an empty desert is low risk.

nodes.label: Paleoclimate
nodes.summary: Ice cores, sediments and isotopes record past climates and CO₂.
nodes.outcome: Read temperature and CO₂ from an ice-core record.
nodes.check: How do ice cores record past temperature and CO₂?
nodes.answer: Trapped air bubbles preserve old atmosphere (CO₂), and oxygen or hydrogen isotope ratios in the ice track temperature.

nodes.label: Geophysical Surveying
nodes.summary: Gravity, magnetic, seismic and electrical methods image the subsurface.
nodes.outcome: Choose a survey method for a buried target.
nodes.check: How can a gravity survey find a buried ore body?
nodes.answer: Dense ore produces a small positive gravity anomaly above it.
